idiom_name: private constructor + #private brand: a type-level guard over JS runtime semantics
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds a compile-time layer over the JavaScript runtime story: a `private constructor` makes `new Foo(...)` outside the class a compile error ('Constructor of class ... is private and only accessible within the class declaration'), which is what stops callers from manufacturing a second instance, and a `#private` (or `private`) member makes instances nominally typed so a look-alike object literal cannot be passed off as the type. Combine it with a static factory, `readonly` fields and a module-private class; note the runtime caveat that these checks are erased - the constructor is still callable from plain JavaScript, and the structured clone algorithm does not carry private elements, so the strongest form remains a `#`-branded instance behind a factory. The classic base-class form has no TypeScript equivalent.
pitfalls: `private` and `private constructor` are erased at runtime: compiled JavaScript can still call the constructor (or `Reflect.construct`), so the guarantee is a type-level guard over an unguarded runtime.

A type-only guard needs the `#` brand: with only `readonly` public fields, a structurally identical object is assignable and a spread/`structuredClone` product can be cast to the class type, then fail at runtime when private state is touched.

Declaration emit strips constructor parameters from private constructors (microsoft/TypeScript#57412), so a factory API typed as `typeof FileHandle` across packages can be incompatible - keep factories in the same module and export a function instead.
`structuredClone`/spread drop the prototype and private fields silently, so the failure appears later as a method error rather than a clear copy rejection.
